The greater sage-grouse, Centrocercus urophasianus, is a large-bodied galliform inhabiting the sagebrush steppe of western North America. Females construct shallow scrapes on the ground, typically laying between 2 and 10 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 10 eggs per clutch], with each hen producing a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year]. Eggs are incubated for a period of 26 days [ab = 26 days] at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], though natural nests may experience minor thermal fluctuations. Hatchlings emerge at a wet weight of approximately 30.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 30.5 grams], a modest initial mass that demands rapid post-hatching development. Chicks achieve first flight and depart the nest around 30 days after hatching [tx = around 30 days after hatching], a milestone that marks the onset of independent mobility but not full nutritional independence. This fledging period is relatively short compared to other lekking tetraonids of similar body mass, likely reflecting the selective pressure to escape ground-based predation during the vulnerable early life stage.

Males of Centrocercus urophasianus exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism, a pattern common among polygynous lekking species. Adult males attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 2300 grams [Wwi = approximately 2300 grams], with typical field records ranging between 1.7 and 2.9 kilograms, whereas females reach a substantially smaller ultimate wet weight of around 1400 grams [Wwi = around 1400 grams], consistent with published accounts placing female mass between 1 and 1.8 kilograms. This size disparity is established early in development, as male chicks exhibit faster growth trajectories and prolonged periods of somatic investment before reaching asymptotic mass. The physiological demands of maintaining such a large body are considerable, and adult males must accumulate substantial lipid reserves during the brief growing season to sustain the energetic costs of lek attendance and courtship display. By contrast, the smaller body size of females may facilitate a higher allocation of resources toward egg production and brood rearing, a classic life-history trade-off observed across many avian taxa.

The timing of developmental milestones in the greater sage-grouse follows a predictable sequence shaped by seasonal resource availability. Puberty, defined here as the age at which broods naturally break up and chicks attain functional independence from their mothers, occurs approximately 12 weeks after hatching [tp = approximately 12 weeks after hatching], or roughly 84 days post-hatching. Field observations of juvenile behavior indicate that young birds begin dispersing from the maternal brood between 10 and 12 weeks of age, coinciding with the progressive atrophy of the brood patch and a decline in parental attentiveness. First reproduction in this species, however, is deferred until the following breeding season, with the time since birth at first reproduction being approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days]. This delay reflects the necessity of completing skeletal growth, acquiring sufficient body condition, and navigating the social hierarchy of the lek before a young male or female can successfully breed.

Longevity records for Centrocercus urophasianus indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 2555 days [am = approximately 2555 days], equivalent to about seven years in the wild, though few individuals attain this upper bound due to high predation pressure, winter harshness, and habitat fragmentation. The oldest grouse in lek-capture datasets rarely exceed that age, with most mortality concentrated in the first year of life. Incubating eggs at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] is critical for normal embryogenesis, as deviations from that temperature can prolong or truncate the incubation window. Beyond incubation, the species' basal metabolic demands scale predictably with body size, and the comparatively long development time to fledging relative to other galliforms may be linked to the nutritional quality of sagebrush forage. Recent population surveys suggest that adult survival is sensitive to drought conditions, which reduce the availability of forbs and insects that hens rely on during the pre-laying period.

Comparative life-history data place Centrocercus urophasianus at the slow end of the fast-slow continuum among North American galliforms, characterized by its single annual clutch of 2 to 10 eggs, delayed maturity until the second year, and a relatively extended potential lifespan of seven years. Hatchlings weighing approximately 30.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 30.5 grams] must nearly double their mass within the first two weeks to survive, and those that reach the independent juvenile stage face a protracted period of learning to locate winter food patches. As a species of conservation concern, understanding these demographic parameters is essential for modeling population viability under changing climatic scenarios and for prioritizing habitat restoration efforts that maintain the thermal refugia and forage diversity upon which this iconic grouse depends.
